summary: Describes and lists the functional requirements of a federated file system, and defines related terms. A federated file system lets file servers present a single namespace to clients. It is not a standards-track document; it is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine many filing cabinets in different rooms that all appear to be one big cabinet. This document lists what such a system must be able to do.

subtitle: A unified filesystem namespace across independent file servers.

tldr.problem: Organizations have multiple independent file servers that clients must navigate separately, making it hard to present a unified namespace. Different servers use different storage systems and administrators.
tldr.mechanism: A federated system defines filesets (abstract directories) with globally unique names (FSNs), and a namespace database (NSDB) that maps these names to physical locations (FSLs). Junctions link directories across filesets, and clients find them through referrals.
tldr.outcome: Applications see a single coherent filesystem hierarchy even though data lives on different servers and administrators, with transparent migration and replication support.

facts.label: Key abstraction
facts.value: Fileset (a directory tree with a unique name)

today: RFC 5716 is Informational, not a standards-track specification. It defines requirements that actual federated file system protocols (such as those in NFS or later TRILL work) can implement. The concepts remain relevant for distributed storage and namespace design.

sections.title: Unified Namespace Across Servers
sections.content:
RFC 5716 defines requirements for a federated file system: a network of independent file servers that present a single, unified namespace to client applications. Without federation, applications must know which server holds which files. With it, clients see one consistent directory tree.

The core idea uses three concepts: a fileset is the abstract unit of storage (roughly a directory tree), an FSN (fileset name) is a globally unique, server-independent identifier for that fileset, and an FSL (fileset location) is the physical server and path where the fileset lives. A junction is a directory link that points from one fileset to another via its FSN.
sections.plainLanguage: A fileset is like a labeled box of files, an FSN is the label, and an FSL is the shelf it sits on. A junction is a sign that points to another box by its label, not by exactly where the shelf is.

sections.title: The Namespace Database Service
sections.content:
The NSDB (namespace database) is the glue holding the system together. It maps each FSN to one or more FSLs, enabling the federation to locate filesets. The NSDB is not a single server; it is a service that can be distributed across multiple NSDB nodes, each responsible for a partition of the namespace.

When a client traverses a junction, the server consults the NSDB to discover where the target fileset lives, then tells the client to access that location directly. This separation of concerns lets different teams manage the file servers and the directory independently.
sections.plainLanguage: The NSDB is like a phone book that translates fileset names into shelf locations. When you follow a junction (a sign), the system looks up the name in the phone book to find the actual server.

sections.title: Junctions and Referrals
sections.content:
A junction is how one fileset links to another. It is a special directory entry that stores only the target fileset's FSN, not its physical location. When a client accesses a junction, the server looks up that FSN in the NSDB, gets back one or more FSLs, and sends the client a referral: a message telling the client to access the file at a new server.

Junctions enable transparent migration: if a fileset moves to a different server, only the NSDB mapping changes, not the junctions pointing to it. They also enable replication: multiple FSLs can share the same FSN, and clients can access any of them.
sections.plainLanguage: A junction is a sign that says 'Look for this under FSN X'. The sign never changes, but where FSN X points to can move or have copies in different places.

sections.title: Core Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies 15 core requirements and several non-requirements. Key mandates include: FSNs must be globally unique and invariant across migration and replication; the NSDB must support creation and deletion of junctions; FSL migration and replication must be manageable through the federation interfaces without changing existing client protocols like NFSv4 or CIFS.

Notably, the requirements do not mandate transaction semantics across NSDB operations, consistency across all client views, or any specific knowledge a client must have of the federation structure. Administrators can define multiple separate namespaces within one federation, and clients discover information as they traverse.
sections.plainLanguage: The main rules are: FSN names never change, the system must support moving and copying filesets, and existing file protocols like NFS must still work without modification.

sections.title: Security and Federation Design
sections.content:
Security requirements focus on protecting communication between servers and NSDB nodes: confidentiality (encryption), data integrity (detection of tampering), and peer authentication (verifying identities). The RFC suggests TLS (for LDAP-based NSDBs) or RPCSEC_GSS (for RPC-based implementations) to satisfy these requirements.

The distributed authorization model is a feature: different administrators can control different parts of the federation without unified identity or privilege. FSNs are long-lived, so creating them should be carefully controlled. The RFC also notes that directory records can track (non-authoritatively) which junctions reference each FSN, aiding administrators.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep conversations between servers and the directory server secret and tamper-proof. Different teams can run different parts of the system with their own rules.
